Bica, cimbalino or expresso-standart expresso
Curto (short)- less than 30 ml

Italiana (italiano or ristretto)-really short coffee as our Italians friends like 10ml

Expresso in a cold cup (usually cup kept in a freezer)

Carioca de café- café poured from a basket that already took an expresso, it becomes a lighter more diluted coffee.
Abatanado ou americano-coffe poured on a capuccino cup.
Com cheirinho (with smell)-expresso with a little bit of an strong alcoholic drink.

I know things vary by region; but as an Australian I feel the need to say how a flat white is served here: single shot of coffee (about 28ml) in a small cup (about 180ml) with steamed milk but the foam is held back.

Here’s the origin incase anyone is interested:
It’s cultural here for people to “call in for a cuppa” which is to visit someone’s home to chat and have a cup of tea or coffee together. In most people’s homes, community centres, sports clubs and other places people gather there will be an electric kettle in the kitchen and next to the kettle will be three jars or containers: one for teabags of generic black tea, one for instant coffee, and one for sugar. When getting drinks ready the conversation usually goes something like this:
Host: “I’m putting the kettle on, what can I get you?”
Guest: “Coffee thanks”
Host: “How do you have it?”
Guest: “White and one”
‘White and one’ means a white coffee (instant coffee with hot water and milk) and one teaspoon of sugar.
In the early days of café culture down here people would be confused by all the different names for coffee drinks as most only knew coffee like you’d get at someone’s house - that led to customers at cafés regularly requesting “I don’t want a frothy coffee, just a flat white”

A latte here is the same ratio and volume as a flat white: 1 shot of espresso with steamed milk but it is served in a glass. The difference here between a flat white and a latte is that a latte has textured milk that results in about 1cm of foam as the milk settles after being poured; so it’s served in a glass so the barista and customer can check to see if the milk has been textured/steamed correctly.

We have a drink called the “Magic” which is similar to what this video calls a flat white; it’s is a double ristretto served in a cup filled 3/4 full with textured/steamed milk in a latte style. However a Magic is kinda like a secret menu item and is usually only known by baristas in trendy cafés.

The only coffe types that can be universally categorized are the original italian ones:
- Espresso: regular coffee shot (~20/30ml)
- Ristretto: a very short espresso (~10/15ml to taste)
- Caffe' lungo: an espresso left running for a little longer (~40/50ml, to taste)
- Macchiato: espresso with a little bit of milk foam
- Cappuccino: an espresso with a little more than 100ml of milk foam
- Latte macchiato: a glass of milk with an espresso shot in (no foam)

This is the undebatable gold standard that is found across italy since 150 years.
If you ask for anything else it will depend on what you want and who makes it.

All the rest are some inventions made around the world (or in Italy itself), that will vary according to region, country, bar, client taste and anything else. It makes no sense to try and define the rules for things that are recent inventions, which will eventually change and vary everywhere (talking about mocaccino, marocchino, flat white, caffe' latte, americano, not to mention the amazing invention of the "Latte" which means simply milk in Italian, and something with a lot of stuff in in English. But there are many more)

- American coffee: the typical American coffee, very long and watery

- macchiato: espresso shot w a dollop of foam
-cortado: an espresso shot with latte milk in a small cup
-flat white: a ristritto shot (pulled for 17 seconds instead of 22-26) with latte milk with very little foam

-cappuccino: espresso w foam milk… can vary on how dry the customer likes it but you mostly give the milk air while you steam it so you get a thick foam that can stand on its own (isn’t runny)

Hmmm I don't think is a good explanation... you need to talk about the difference in the milk, and the milk to espresso ratios.

Cappucino, latte and flat white can all have the same amount of espresso.

- Latte has a relatively large amount of milk, steamed to a silky microfoam. Espresso taste is more diluted.
- Cappuccino has less milk, but steamed/stretched to the same volume as the latte. It is stiffer and less silky. Doesn't have latte art as the milk is too stiff. Often dusted with choc or cinnamon. Coffee is less diluted than the latte. What they showed here wasn't really a cappuccino, it had silky milk.
- Flat white has similar espresso to milk ratio as a cappuccino, but the milk is steamed to microfoam only. This makes it a smaller drink. You can put latte art on it, as the foam isn't stiff. It has similar espresso flavor as the cappuccino, due to similar dilution, but has a silkier mouthfeel due to the microfoamed milk.

The exact size of each drink isn't what's important here, nor whether it's single or double shot. It's the qualities of the drinks relative to each other that is important. I.e. milk steaming and dilution of espresso with the milk.
